turns.content: Five families splitting a $2,500 cabin. That means 500 flat each right

Yep — $2,500 ÷ 5 = $500 per family, nice and clean.

Only wrinkle worth a thought: "flat each" assumes everyone's okay splitting evenly regardless of family size or who gets the master bedroom vs. the pullout couch. If everybody's cool with even, $500 it is. If someone's a party of two and another's a party of six, you might hear grumbling — but that's a group-chat problem, not a math problem.
Lodge just sent a binding addendum. One room flooded so that family got cut to 100. Other four rooms re-invoiced at 600 each to hit 2500 total.

The math checks: $100 + (4 × $600) = $2,500. Adds up exactly.

But notice what that actually does: the lodge didn't take a hit for the flood — the other four families did. Each of them is now paying $100 more to cover the $400 discount the flooded family got. The lodge's total revenue is unchanged.

A flooded room is a lodge problem, not a your-group problem. If a room isn't usable, the normal outcome is the lodge eats that loss (or offers a comparable room/refund), not that the remaining guests get re-invoiced upward. Also, "binding addendum" is doing a lot of work there — a change to an existing agreement generally needs both sides to agree to it, so it's worth checking your original booking terms before anyone pays the $600.

Reasonable ask: "We'll pay $2,100 total ($500 × 4 usable rooms, plus $100 for the partial room) — or the original $2,500 if you can provide a fifth usable room."
So you told me 500 flat for everyone. I sent the group message billing 500 each. Now what do I tell them about the lodge's 600 invoice

Quick reality check first: $500 was right when you sent it — the lodge changed the deal after the fact. Your message wasn't wrong; the situation moved underneath it. Nobody's going to blame you for not predicting a flood.

What to tell the group depends on which path you want to take, so pick one before you type:

**Option A — you're going to push back on the lodge (recommended)**

Send a short heads-up so nobody's blindsided, but don't ask for more money yet:

> "Update: one room at the cabin flooded. The lodge is trying to re-invoice the other four rooms at $600 to make up the difference. I don't think that's on us — I'm pushing back with them now. Hold at $500 for the moment; I'll update once they respond."

This keeps you in control and doesn't lock anyone into a number that might change again.

**Option B — the group just wants it settled and the $100 isn't worth the fight**

> "Update: one room flooded, and the lodge dropped that family's share to $100. To keep the total at $2,500 they've asked the rest of us for $600 each — an extra $100. Not thrilled about it, but if everyone's fine absorbing it, I'll confirm. Shout if you'd rather I contest it first."

**Either way, don't send the $600 number as final yet.** Once you tell four families "it's $600," it's very hard to walk back if the lodge later agrees to $500. Contest first, bill second.

And when you talk to the lodge, the framing is simple: you booked five rooms at $2,500, they can only deliver four and a half, so the price should go *down*, not stay flat with a reshuffle. Ask them to point to the clause in your original agreement that lets them unilaterally re-price the other rooms.
I pushed back on the lodge. They held firm on 600 per room. So now what. I send the group a new number or eat the difference myself

Don't eat it. $400 out of your pocket for a flood you didn't cause and a lodge you didn't design is a bad trade, and it sets a precedent where you're the shock absorber for the whole group. Send the group the new number.

Before you do, two things worth checking quickly:

- **Escalation:** If this was booked through a platform (Airbnb/VRBO/etc.) or paid by credit card, that's your leverage — a "you can only deliver four usable rooms but want full price" complaint usually gets traction there. Worth one more shot in parallel, but don't hold the group hostage waiting on it.
- **The internal split is yours, not the lodge's.** The lodge cares about $2,500 total. How the five of you divide it is a group decision. Right now the lodge's allocation has four families covering the flooded family's $400 discount. Is the flooded family still coming? Are they bunking in someone else's room? If they're still getting a bed, an even $500 all around might be fairer than $100/$600 — worth a sentence to the group rather than assuming.

Draft:

> "Update on the cabin: I pushed back on the lodge over the flooded room, and they wouldn't budge — total's still $2,500. Their invoice has the flooded room at $100 and the other four at $600. That's $100 more than I told you earlier, and I'm sorry for the change — the lodge moved the goalposts after the fact. I'm still going to try [platform/card] as a last resort, but plan on $600 for now. If anyone thinks we should split it differently among ourselves (e.g., evening it out depending on where the fifth family ends up sleeping), say so and we'll sort it out."

Own the number change, blame the lodge (accurately), keep the door open for the group to redistribute. Nobody reasonable is going to be mad at the messenger.
So I send the group 600 now or do I push one more time with the lodge

Both — but not sequenced. Send the group now, and take one more run at the lodge in parallel.

**Why send now:** The group has been holding at $500 based on your last message. Every day they don't know, the eventual "actually it's $600" lands harder. Telling them "plan on $600, I'm still working it" costs nothing and removes the surprise. If you later win the argument, refunding $100 to four people is a good problem to have.

**Why the second push is only worth it if something changes:** Asking the same person the same question again gets the same answer. A second attempt should be different in at least one way:

- **Go up a level** — ask for a manager/owner, not the front desk or whoever sent the addendum.
- **Change the channel** — if this was booked via a platform or paid by credit card, go through them. "Property can only deliver four of five rooms at full price" is a straightforward complaint.
- **Change the ask** — instead of "lower the total," try "provide a fifth usable room" or "give the flooded family a credit for a future stay." Sometimes they'll bend on a different lever.
- **Put it in writing** — a short email stating you never agreed to the addendum and the original booking was five rooms for $2,500 creates a paper trail if this goes to a chargeback later.

If none of those levers exist — it's a direct booking, you paid by check, the person you talked to *is* the owner — then skip the second push. You've done the due diligence, and it's just $600.

One practical thing: when's payment actually due? If there's a few days of slack, that's your window for the escalation. If it's due tomorrow, send the $600 message today and treat any refund as a bonus.
